Fundamental Linear Algebra:
Matrix: A rectangular array of numbers, symbols, or expressions arranged in rows and columns.<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 4>
Linear Transform: A function that maps vectors from one vector space to another, satisfying $T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v)$ and $T(cu) = cT(u)$ for all vectors $u$, $v$ and scalars $c$.<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 5><L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 6>
Matrix Multiplication: An operation that combines two matrices to produce a third matrix, where the element at row $i$ and column $j$ of the resulting matrix is the dot product of the $i$-th row of the first matrix and the $j$-th column of the second matrix. The inner dimensions must match.<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 14><L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 15>
Matrix Inverse: For a square matrix $A$, its inverse $A^{-1}$ is a matrix such that $AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I$, where $I$ is the identity matrix.<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 10>
Matrix Transposition: An operation that swaps the rows and columns of a matrix.  The transpose of matrix $A$ is denoted as $A^T$.<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 16>
Derivative: A measure of how a function changes with respect to a change in its input. <L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 21>
Partial Derivative: A derivative of a function of multiple variables with respect to one of those variables, holding the others constant.<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 19>
Sigmoid Function: A mathematical function having a characteristic "S"-shaped curve, often used as an activation function in neural networks. Its derivative is shown in slide 21.<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 21>

Matrix Factorization: A technique that decomposes a large matrix into the product of two smaller matrices, revealing latent factors that capture underlying relationships in the data.<L[11L2-svd-pca-recommender] 2><L[11L2-svd-pca-recommender] 3><L[11L2-svd-pca-recommender] 4><L[11L2-svd-pca-recommender] 5><L[11L2-svd-pca-recommender] 13><L[11L2-svd-pca-recommender] 36>

Examples include clustering documents, images, genes, and movies. <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 4><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 6><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 7><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 8><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 9><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 10>

Defining and Applying K-means Clustering: Partitioning objects into $K$ disjoint subsets using a distance measure (typically Euclidean distance: $d_E(x, y) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^p (x_i - y_i)^2}$) between $p$-dimensional vectors.  The algorithm iteratively assigns points to the nearest cluster mean and updates the means until convergence. <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 21><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 22><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 31>

Evaluating Clustering Results: Assessing the "goodness" of resulting clusters, either subjectively (visual inspection of proximity matrices and PCA-reduced visualizations) or objectively (using known class labels and metrics like purity). <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 32><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 33><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 38><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 39><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 40><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 41><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 44><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 45>

Understanding Distance Measures:  Using appropriate distance measures (Euclidean distance for continuous data, Hamming distance for discrete data) to quantify the similarity or dissimilarity between data points. <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 17><L[12L2-distance-clusters] 19>

Linear Algebra:
Matrix Addition: $A + B = C$, where $c_{ij} = a_{ij} + b_{ij}$<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 9>

Matrix Scalar Multiplication: $k \cdot A = B$, where $b_{ij} = k \cdot a_{ij}$<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 9>

Matrix Multiplication: $C_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{ik}b_{kj}$<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 14>

Matrix Inverse: $AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I$<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 10>

Solving Linear Equations using Matrix Inverses: $Ax = b \implies x = A^{-1}b$<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 12>
Machine Learning Fundamentals:
Linear Regression: Find the line that minimizes the sum of squared distances between the data points and the line.  This is done by minimizing the following equation with respect to $w$ and $l$: $\min_{w,l} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (ws_i + l - p_i)^2$.  The solution is given by $w^* = \frac{\sigma^2_{SP}}{\sigma^2_{SS}}$, $l^* = \bar{P} - w^*\bar{S}$, where $\bar{P} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} p_i$, $\bar{S} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} s_i$, $\sigma^2_{SP} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(s_i - \bar{S})(p_i - \bar{P})$, and $\sigma^2_{SS} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(s_i - \bar{S})^2$.<L[05L2-ML Basics] 9><L[05L2-ML Basics] 10>

Multiple Linear Regression:  Find the optimal coefficients $\beta^*$ that minimize the sum of squared errors between the observed and predicted values. This is achieved by solving the equation $\beta^* = (X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty$, where $y$ is the vector of observed values, $X$ is the design matrix of independent variables, and $\beta$ is the vector of coefficients.<L[05L2-ML Basics] 11><L[05L2-ML Basics] 16>

Regularized Linear Regression: $E(w) = RSS(w) + \lambda R(w)$, where $R(w)$ is either $||w||_2^2$ or $||w||_1$, and $\lambda$ controls the trade-off between training error and complexity.<L[10L1-CrossValidation] 17>

S-fold Cross Validation: Split the training data into $S$ equal parts; use each part as a validation dataset and the others as a training dataset; choose the hyperparameter leading to the best average performance.<L[10L1-CrossValidation] 25>


Fairness through Blindness: Ignore protected attributes during model training and prediction. <L[16L2-ethics] 25>

Group Fairness: $P(\text{outcome } o | S) = P(\text{outcome } o | T)$, where $S$ and $T$ are two groups.  This is insufficient as a fairness metric. <L[16L2-ethics] 26>

Individual Fairness: Treat similar individuals similarly; similar individuals should have similar outcomes.  How to achieve this is an open research question. <L[16L2-ethics] 27>

Detecting and Removing Bias from Models: Keep bias features in the data during training, then remove what was learned from these features after training. <L[16L2-ethics] 34>
Classification Algorithms:
Binary Classification using Linear Models:  Use a linear model $w^Tx$ to predict the label. The sign of $w^Tx$ determines the predicted label: $+1$ if $w^Tx > 0$, and $-1$ if $w^Tx \le 0$.<L[05L2-ML Basics] 24>

Perceptron Algorithm: Iteratively update the weight vector $w$ by adding $y_nx_n$ if the data point $x_n$ is misclassified (i.e., $\text{sign}(w^Tx_n) \ne y_n$).<L[05L2-ML Basics] 30>

Logistic Regression:  Use a linear model $w^Tx$ and the sigmoid function $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$ to predict the probability of a data point belonging to a class. The weight vector $w$ is updated iteratively using stochastic gradient descent: $w \leftarrow w + \alpha(\sigma(-y_nw^Tx_n)y_nx_n)$, where $\alpha$ is the learning rate.<L[05L2-ML Basics] 32><L[05L2-ML Basics] 33>


Bag of Features: Represent images by frequencies of "visual words" (Bags of features)<L[07L2-Vision] 16>

Nearest Neighbor Classifier: Assign label of nearest training data point to each test data point<L[07L2-Vision] 30>
Neural Networks:
Derivative of Sigmoid Function: $\frac{d}{dx} \sigma(x) = \frac{e^{-x}}{(1 + e^{-x})^2}$<L[04L1-Linear Algebra Primer] 21>


ReLU Activation Function: A piecewise linear activation function defined as $f(x) = \max(0, x)$, introducing non-linearity into the network. <L[09L1-cnn] 13>

Backpropagation Algorithm: An algorithm used to train neural networks by calculating the gradient of the loss function with respect to the network's weights and updating the weights iteratively to minimize the loss. <L[09L1-cnn] 16>

Max Pooling: A pooling operation that selects the maximum value within a defined region (e.g., 2x2) of a feature map, reducing the spatial dimensions while preserving the depth. <L[09L1-cnn] 14><L[09L1-cnn] 15>

Average Pooling: A pooling operation that calculates the average value within a defined region (e.g., 2x2) of a feature map, reducing the spatial dimensions while preserving the depth. <L[09L1-cnn] 15>

LeNet-5 Architecture: A specific CNN architecture designed for the MNIST dataset, consisting of convolutional layers, pooling layers, and fully connected layers. <L[09L1-cnn] 22>
Image Processing:
Moving Average Filter: Replace each pixel with an average of all the values in its neighborhood<L[07L2-Vision] 38><L[07L2-Vision] 39>

Weighted Moving Average Filter: Add weights to the moving average to give different importance to neighboring pixels<L[07L2-Vision] 40><L[07L2-Vision] 41>

Image Sharpening: $f_{sharp} = f + \alpha(f - f_{blur})$ where $f$ is the original image, $f_{blur}$ is the blurred image, and $\alpha$ is a scaling factor<L[07L2-Vision] 55>


Finite Difference Method: $\frac{df}{dx} [x, y] \approx F[x + 1, y] - F[x, y]$<L[08L2-Feature Extraction] 15>

Image Gradient Magnitude: $||\nabla f|| = \sqrt{(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x})^2 + (\frac{\partial f}{\partial y})^2}$<L[08L2-Feature Extraction] 17>

Image Gradient Direction: $\theta = \tan^{-1}(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} / \frac{\partial f}{\partial y})$<L[08L2-Feature Extraction] 34>

Anisotropic Gaussian: $G_{\sigma_x, \sigma_y}(x, y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_x\sigma_y} \cdot e^{-\frac{1}{2}((\frac{x^2}{\sigma_x^2}) + (\frac{y^2}{\sigma_y^2}))}$<L[08L2-Feature Extraction] 43>

Isotropic Gaussian: $G_\sigma(x, y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2} \cdot e^{-\frac{r^2}{2\sigma^2}}$<L[08L2-Feature Extraction] 43>
Search Algorithms:
Minimax Search: A recursive algorithm for two-player zero-sum games that explores the game tree to find the best move for the current player, assuming the opponent also plays optimally.  It alternates between maximizing the score for the current player and minimizing the score for the opponent.<L[02L2-Intro] 22>

Alpha-Beta Pruning: An optimization technique for Minimax search that reduces the search space by avoiding the evaluation of branches that cannot affect the optimal decision. It uses alpha and beta values to prune branches.<L[02L2-Intro] 23>


Recursive Binary Search Tree Search:  Recursively check the current node's value ($V$) against the target value ($X$). If $V == X$, return `True`. If $X < V$, recursively search the left subtree; if $X > V$, recursively search the right subtree. If no children exist, return `False`.<L[14L1-DepthFS] 10>

Breadth-First Search: Explore nodes level by level, adding children to a queue.<L[14L1-DepthFS] 8>

Depth-First Search: Explore a branch completely before moving to another branch.<L[14L1-DepthFS] 8>
Recommender Systems:
Collaborative Filtering: Predicts a user's rating for an item based on the ratings of similar users.  Key steps: 1. Find similar users; 2. Aggregate similar users' ratings for the item; 3. Predict the user's rating.<L[11L2-svd-pca-recommender] 33>

Matrix Factorization for Recommender Systems: Approximates a user-item rating matrix as a product of two lower-dimensional matrices representing user and item latent factors.  $r_{i,j} \approx u_i \cdot v_j$, where $r_{i,j}$ is the rating of user $i$ for item $j$, $u_i$ is the user's latent factor vector, and $v_j$ is the item's latent factor vector.<L[11L2-svd-pca-recommender] 36>

Modeling Systematic Biases in Recommender Systems: $r_{ij} \approx \mu + b_i + b_j + u_i \cdot v_j$, where $r_{ij}$ is the rating, $\mu$ is the overall mean rating, $b_i$ is the user bias, $b_j$ is the item bias, and $u_i \cdot v_j$ represents user-item interactions.<L[11L2-svd-pca-recommender] 44>
Clustering Algorithms:
K-means Clustering:  The algorithm iteratively assigns data points to the nearest cluster centroid, then recomputes the centroids as the mean of the points in each cluster, repeating until convergence. <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 22>

Euclidean Distance: $d_E(x, y) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{p} (x_i - y_i)^2}$, where $x$ and $y$ are $p$-dimensional vectors. <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 17>

Hamming Distance: Counts the number of differing bits between two binary vectors. <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 19>

Matching Coefficient:  Hamming distance normalized by the number of attributes/bits. <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 19>

Purity: $purity(C, G) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{K} \max_{j} N_j \in G_i$, where $N$ is the total number of data points, $K$ is the number of clusters, and $N_j$ is the number of points of class $j$ in cluster $i$. <L[12L2-distance-clusters] 44>
SAT Solving:
DPLL Algorithm: A backtracking-based algorithm for solving the Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT). It systematically assigns truth values to variables, checking for contradictions and backtracking when necessary. <L[13L1-Logic] 15><L[13L1-Logic] 16><L[13L1-Logic] 17><L[13L1-Logic] 19><L[13L1-Logic] 24>

Conversion to CNF: A set of rules to transform any logical expression into an equivalent Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF) expression.  This is crucial for using SAT solvers, as many solvers are designed to work specifically with CNF. <L[13L1-Logic] 17><L[13L1-Logic] 18>


DPLL: A recursive algorithm that improves upon the Naïve\_SAT algorithm by incorporating Boolean Constraint Propagation (BCP) to efficiently identify and resolve unit clauses, significantly reducing the search space.<L[15L2-SAT] 17>

BCP: A sub-algorithm within DPLL that repeatedly identifies and assigns values to literals in unit clauses (clauses with only one unassigned literal), creating a cascading effect that simplifies the formula and often leads to quicker conflict detection.<L[15L2-SAT] 20>

Resolution Rule: An inference rule that derives a new clause from two existing clauses containing a literal and its negation.  The new clause combines the remaining literals from the original clauses using logical OR.<L[15L2-SAT] 32>

Clause Learning: A technique used to learn from conflicts encountered during the DPLL search.  When a conflict occurs, a concise reason (a clause) is learned to prevent similar conflicts in the future, improving efficiency.<L[15L2-SAT] 35>

Hamiltonian Path Encoding:  A method to encode the Hamiltonian Path Problem into a SAT problem.  It uses Boolean variables $h_{ij}$ representing whether the $i$-th vertex visited is vertex $j$.  Constraints are added to ensure the path uses only existing edges and visits each vertex exactly once.<L[15L2-SAT] 46>

Graph Coloring Encoding: A method to encode the Graph Coloring Problem into a SAT problem.  It uses Boolean variables to represent the assignment of colors to vertices, with constraints ensuring that adjacent vertices have different colors.<L[15L2-SAT] 47><L[15L2-SAT] 48><L[15L2-SAT] 49>
